T1: Consumers will adopt lawn tractors if they perceive them as a convenient, low-cost solution for small garden chores, and Deere can capture value by selling directly to consumers through a new channel. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and small garden owners who need a low-cost, easy-to-use tool for light landscaping.. Why behaviour changes: Growing household garden size and interest in DIY in the 1960s make a small, affordable tractor attractive; consumers will purchase if they see it as a practical, low-maintainance option.. How value is captured: Deere sells tractors directly to consumers at retail price, bypassing dealers, and can charge a premium for brand reputation and quality.. Assumptions: Consumer survey data from 1962 shows interest in garden tractors among households.; Deere can produce a reliable, affordable model within existing tractor engineering.; Retail distribution is feasible without disrupting the existing B2B2C model.. Predictions: If a test offers a direct-to-consumer lawn tractor at a price point comparable to existing garden tools, purchase intent will be higher than when sold through dealers.; Sales volume will increase in markets where garden equipment is already popular, such as the Midwest and Northeast..

T2: Consumers will adopt lawn tractors if they view them as a status symbol or status-enhancing tool, and Deere can capture value by positioning tractors as premium, brand‑rich products sold through a new direct‑to‑consumer channel. Who benefits: Affluent homeowners and early adopters who seek to signal success or status through ownership of modern, brand‑rich equipment.. Why behaviour changes: In the 1960‑s, ownership of a lawn tractor became a visible marker of modernity and success; consumers will purchase if they perceive the tractor as a status item rather than just a utility tool.. How value is captured: Deere sells tractors at a premium price through its own retail outlets, leveraging brand prestige and limited edition features to justify higher margins.. Assumptions: Status and brand perception were important purchase drivers for high‑end consumer goods in 1962.; Deere can produce a lawn tractor that meets or exceeds the aesthetic and performance expectations of a status item.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a brand associated with quality and modernity.. Predictions: If a test offers a premium‑priced lawn tractor with brand‑focused marketing, purchase intent will be higher among affluent households compared to a standard‑priced model.; Sales volume will be concentrated in regions where affluence and early adoption are higher, such as the Northeast and California..

Test "Consumer Messaging Test for Lawn Tractor" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two distinct ad copy versions. Participants view a description of a lawn tractor, either emphasizing low cost and convenience (T1) or emphasizing status and brand prestige (T2). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this tractor if offered at a price comparable to existing garden tools?". Sample: 400 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced for region (Midwest, Northeast, California) and household income (low, moderate, high).. Measure: Purchase intent binary (yes/no) and willingness-to-pay (WTP) on a 0–10 scale.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP when the ad emphasizes low cost and convenience.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP when the ad emphasizes status and brand prestige.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for the low‑cost/convenience version exceeds the status version by at least 15 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners who value convenience. If the difference is <15 points or not significant, consider no expansion.. Cost: 8000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑scale landscaping and homeowner tasks, leveraging existing tractor engineering. Begin with a limited direct‑to‑consumer pilot in high‑garden‑equipment markets (Midwest, Northeast) to test demand before broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer motivations for lawn tractors or the feasibility of a direct-to-consumer proposition. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping and homeowner tasks, leveraging existing tractor engineering. Begin with a limited direct-to-consumer pilot in high-garden-equipment markets (Midwest, Northeast) to test demand before broader rollout. Target customer: Individual homeowners and small garden owners who need a low-cost, easy-to-use tool for light landscaping.. Value proposition: A lawn tractor sold directly to consumers at a price comparable to existing garden tools, offering convenience, reliability, and Deere’s brand reputation, capturing value through retail margins and brand premium.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (400 households, 8 weeks, €8,000) to compare low‑cost/convenience messaging versus status/brand messaging. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer line.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for lawn tractors in 1962 is unknown; the test will reveal whether demand is sufficient to justify investment. Also uncertain is whether consumers will pay a premium for status positioning.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the status version significantly higher than the low‑cost version (difference ≥ 15 percentage points and statistically significant), we would reconsider the proposition and focus on a premium, brand‑dr; If the test yields no significant difference or the low‑cost version outperforms, we would recommend no expansion and continue the existing B2B2C model.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lifestyle vs Medical Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message frames: lifestyle (e.g., “Protect your hearing while enjoying the outdoors”) or medical (e.g., “Meeting legal safety standards for hearing protection”). They view a product description of a hearing protector meeting EN 352 standards and are asked: “How much would you pay for this product?”. Sample: 500 adults aged 18–65 in Europe, recruited via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.. Measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for the product described under each message frame.. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle frame will generate a WTP at least 20% higher than the medical frame.; T2: Medical frame will generate a WTP at least 15% higher than the lifestyle frame.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the lifestyle frame exceeds the average WTP for the medical frame by at least 20% (i.e., lifestyle ≥ × 1.2 – medical ≤ × 0.8), then T1 is supported and the recommendation is to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing lifestyle. If the medical frame exceeds the lifestyle frame by at least 15%, then T2 is supported and the recommendation is to develop a differentiated proposition emphasizing medical necessity. If neither difference meets the thresholds, the recommendation is to “. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory for outdoor recreation and personal safety, rather than as a medical necessity. Begin with a limited launch of a design‑focused product marketed through specialty retailers and direct‑to‑consumer channels, using the existing Hellberg brand and distribution network. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-B shows that a softer, better-fitting protector did not increase wear frequency compared to a standard one. This contradicts T1’s prediction that comfort and design would drive higher adoption. Therefore T1 is not supported by this evidence. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a medical necessity for specific health risks (e.g., noise-induced hearing loss).. Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory for outdoor recreation and personal safety, rather than as a medical necessity. Begin with a limited launch of a design‑focused product marketed through specialty retailers and direct‑to‑consumer channels, using the existing Hellberg brand and distribution network. Target customer: Outdoor enthusiasts, musicians, and individuals who value comfort and style during outdoor activities and work.. Value proposition: A hearing protector that combines EN 352 certification with innovative design, offering peace of mind and a stylish accessory that enhances outdoor experiences.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed willingness‑to‑pay survey (or a smaller pilot) to test the impact of lifestyle messaging versus medical messaging, and use the results to decide whether to proceed with a full launch.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited; the survey test is the only direct measure of consumer willingness to pay for a lifestyle proposition. The market size and competitive landscape for lifestyle hearing protection are also uncertain.. Would change if: If the survey shows that medical messaging generates a willingness‑to‑pay premium of at least 15% over lifestyle messaging, or if a pilot launch yields higher sales than expected, the recommendation would shift toward emphasizing medical or; if new independent evidence shows strong consumer demand for hearing protection as a medical necessity, or if a competitor successfully launches a medical‑focused line, the recommendation would shift toward that alternative.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Participants indicate which concept they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay. The test is limited to 500 participants, 12 weeks, and costs €20,000.. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25-55 with a household income above the median, recruited via an online panel. Stratify by geographic region to reflect 1962 U.S. market distribution.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: percentage choosing Concept A over B. 2) Maximum price willingness to pay: average amount participants indicate they would pay for Concept A. 3) Primary purchase reason: open-ended survey question identifying whether participants cite status/convenience (T1) or reliability/ease of use (T2).. Predictions: T1: Concept A will be chosen by at least 55% of participants, and the average price willingness for A will be at least 20% higher than for B.; T2: Concept B will be chosen by at least 55% of participants, and the average price willingness for B will be at least 20% higher than for A.. Decision rule: If Concept A’s purchase intent ≥ 55% and its average price willingness ≥ 20% higher than Concept B, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing status and convenience. If Concept B’s purchase intent ≥ 55% and its average price willingness ≥ 20% higher than A, develop a proposition emphasizing reliability and ease of use. If neither threshold is met, abandon expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.
